finding.claim: Authorization bypass on ban: the admin check in ban() is wrapped in try/except Exception, so the 403 raised by require_admin is swallowed and do_ban(uid) runs for any caller that reaches the route, including non-admins. Any user can ban any other user.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled: an HTTP POST to /admin/users/<uid>/ban by a request whose g.user is a non-admin user dict (is_admin falsy). The uid path parameter is also attacker-chosen (line 15).
finding.sink: do_ban(uid) at admin.py:20 (protected state-changing operation; currently a stub at line 31-32, so real impact depends on its implementation).

trace.note: Route POST /admin/users/<uid>/ban registered; no decorator or login/admin guard on the route itself.
require_admin(g.user) called with the request user.
user.get('is_admin') is falsy for a non-admin.
abort(403) raises werkzeug HTTPException, which subclasses Exception.
except Exception catches the HTTPException, so the 403 is discarded.
Logs a warning and continues instead of returning or re-raising.
Returns jsonify(ok=True) to the non-admin caller.

finding.guards_checked: (1) require_admin's abort(403) at admin.py:11 is the only admin control, and it is neutralised by the broad except at line 18. (2) unban() at admin.py:24-28 calls require_admin outside any try, so it correctly returns 403 and is NOT affected. (3) No before_request hook, decorator, or blueprint-level guard is in this file; g.user population and any login enforcement live outside the provided code and could not be checked. Even if an upstream hook guarantees g.user is an authenticated user, this only enforces authentication, not admin.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. require_admin (admin.py:9-11) does abort(403), but the call at admin.py:17 sits inside try/except Exception (admin.py:16-18). werkzeug's HTTPException subclasses Exception, so the 403 is swallowed. Execution continues to do_ban(uid) at admin.py:20 with no return or re-raise. The route at admin.py:14 has no decorator, and no before_request guard exists in this file. unban() at admin.py:24-28 is not affected because it calls require_admin outside any try.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches admin.py: the 403 raised by abort at admin.py:11 is caught by the broad except at admin.py:18, and do_ban(uid) at admin.py:20 then runs for any caller whose g.user is a dict, so a low-privilege authenticated user can reach it. Two caveats: if g.user is unset, the log line at admin.py:19 raises AttributeError before do_ban runs, and upstream authentication (not in this file) decides who reaches the route. do_ban is a stub here, so real impact depends on its implementation.

finding.claim: The failed-admin-check path logs the caller's name (g.user.get('name')) at warning level, which records a user identifier in logs on every unauthorized ban attempt. This conflicts with the org policy against logging PII.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled-ish: any caller who fails the admin check triggers the log line, and the logged value is the caller's own account name from g.user.

trace.note: log.warning('admin check failed for %s', g.user.get('name')) writes the name to the log.

finding.guards_checked: No redaction or masking of g.user['name'] is present. Whether 'name' is PII depends on what it holds (a real name or email would be PII). Also, if g.user is None the handler itself raises AttributeError on line 19, which surfaces as a 500 instead of a 403; this is a robustness issue, not a security bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none. No redaction or masking of g.user.get('name') exists at admin.py:19. The except at admin.py:18 catches the 403 from require_admin (admin.py:11), so execution reaches the log call. The candidate's claim that the log line runs for failed checks is accurate.
verdict.reason: The log at admin.py:19 writes g.user.get('name') on every failed admin check reached via the except at admin.py:18, with no redaction, so the logging claim holds as stated; whether a display name counts as PII is a judgment call. The more serious defect is that the except at admin.py:18 swallows the abort(403) from admin.py:11, so do_ban(uid) at admin.py:20 runs for non-admins. That is an authorization bypass the candidate did not report, and the candidate's "robustness only" note on the None case does not cover it.
